title: The Parcel That Found Home
scenes: Pip the robot writes a message, but the internet cannot send the whole thing as one enormous parcel.
So Pip splits it into small packets. Each packet carries information that helps it reach the destination.
The packets may travel along different routes. At the other end, software puts the message back together.
The internet is a network of networks. Many small deliveries can become one big conversation.

title: The Name Shop
scenes: Mochi remembers the name of a website, but the delivery robot needs a numerical address.
A DNS resolver helps translate that familiar name into an IP address the computer can use.
Sometimes the answer is already cached nearby. Otherwise, the resolver asks other DNS servers for help.
A website name is like a label in an address book. DNS helps find where to send the request.

title: The Busy Crossing
scenes: Two tiny delivery bots arrive at a junction. Which network should each packet visit next?
The router checks destination addresses and uses its routing information to choose a next step.
It does not need a map of every cable on Earth. It needs a useful next hop.
Routers pass packets between networks, one decision at a time. A long journey becomes many local choices.

title: The Missing Envelope
scenes: Pip sends a drawing, but one packet disappears before it reaches Mochi. The picture has a gap.
With TCP, the receiver can acknowledge delivered data, and missing data can be sent again.
TCP also helps present the bytes in the right order, even when packets arrive out of order.
Reliable delivery takes extra coordination. The internet can recover from a missing piece instead of starting everything again.

title: The Secret Tunnel
scenes: Mochi wants to visit a website without strangers reading the message along the way.
HTTPS uses encryption to protect data travelling between the browser and the server.
Certificates help the browser check the server's identity. But a secure connection does not guarantee an honest website.
Look at both the connection and the destination. A locked tunnel can still lead to a dishonest shop.

title: The Nearby Copy
scenes: Pip asks the same question twice. The second answer arrives much faster. Did the cable suddenly become quicker?
A cache stores a nearby copy of data that may be needed again.
The computer can reuse that copy instead of downloading or calculating everything from the beginning.
Caching saves work, but old copies can become stale. Fast answers still need a way to stay fresh.

title: The Wide Road
scenes: Mochi makes the road wider, yet the first parcel still takes time to arrive. What happened?
Bandwidth describes how much data a connection can carry per second. Latency describes delay.
A wider road can carry more parcels together without making the journey itself shorter.
Speed has more than one meaning. A video download and a live conversation can need different improvements.

title: The Radio Picnic
scenes: Pip takes a laptop into the garden. No cable follows it, but the messages still arrive.
Wi-Fi carries data using radio waves between the device and a nearby access point.
The access point connects that wireless link to a wider network, often through a router.
Wi-Fi is the local wireless connection. The internet is the much larger network it may connect you to.

title: The Two Doors
scenes: Mochi finds two doors on the same server. One leads to the web shop, the other to mail.
An IP address identifies a network destination. A port number helps identify a service at that destination.
Many applications can use the same device because the network keeps track of these separate conversations.
Think of the address as the building and the port as a numbered door inside the network conversation.

title: The Gatekeeper's List
scenes: A strange packet knocks on Pip's network gate. Should the robot let every visitor walk straight in?
A firewall checks network traffic against rules. Some traffic is allowed, and some is blocked.
Rules can consider details such as addresses, ports, and connection state. They must match the network's needs.
A firewall is one layer of protection. Sensible rules and updated software still matter behind the gate.

title: The Desk and the Cupboard
scenes: Pip puts every notebook on a tiny desk. Soon there is no room left to work.
RAM is the computer's working memory. Storage keeps files for longer, including when the power is off.
Ordinary RAM loses its contents without power. Saving a document writes a lasting copy to storage.
A larger desk helps with active work. A larger cupboard helps keep more things. Computers need both.

title: The Recipe Runner
scenes: Mochi gives a robot a recipe. It follows the instructions, one useful operation after another.
A CPU executes instructions and coordinates much of the computer's general work.
Its cores can handle separate streams of work, but programs must be designed to benefit from them.
More cores do not make every task equally faster. Some recipes still contain steps that must happen in order.

title: The Paint Crew
scenes: Pip hires one artist to colour thousands of tiles. The artist is clever, but the wall takes ages.
A GPU can perform many similar calculations in parallel. That suits graphics and some scientific or AI tasks.
It still needs data and instructions. Not every program can be turned into thousands of independent little jobs.
Choose the right worker for the work. A paint crew shines when many tiles can be painted together.

title: The Fast Little Drawer
scenes: Mochi keeps walking to a distant shelf for the same tool. Pip adds a drawer beside the desk.
A CPU cache stores small amounts of frequently needed data close to the processor.
Fetching nearby data is often faster than waiting for data from farther away in the memory system.
The drawer is small, so it cannot hold everything. Good organisation helps the processor spend less time waiting.

title: The Tiny Light Switch
scenes: Pip needs a simple way to record two possibilities. A little lamp can be off or on.
A bit represents one of two values, usually written as zero and one.
Groups of bits can represent numbers, text, images, or instructions, depending on how software interprets them.
Eight bits make a byte. Simple choices become powerful when we agree on how to combine and read them.

title: The Stage Manager
scenes: Three robot musicians all want the microphone, the screen, and the same notebook. The stage becomes chaos.
An operating system manages resources such as processing time, memory, files, and devices.
It provides services that applications use, and it helps keep separate programs from interfering with each other.
The operating system is the stage manager. Applications can perform because something coordinates the shared equipment.

title: The Saved Drawing
scenes: Mochi finishes a drawing and closes the app. Tomorrow the picture is gone. Was remembering the same as saving?
While editing, an application may keep changes in working memory. Saving writes them to a file.
Some apps save automatically, but the timing and destination depend on the app.
Before closing important work, check that it was saved where you expect. A finished thought needs a lasting home.

title: The Library With Labels
scenes: Pip puts a thousand files in one pile. Finding the right story becomes the hardest job of all.
A file system organises stored data into files and directories, with names and other information.
The folder you see is an organisation tool, not necessarily one continuous physical box on the drive.
Good names and folders help humans too. Storage is more useful when both the computer and the reader can find things.

title: The Hot Robot
scenes: Mochi works so hard that the little robot grows warm. Pip adds a fan and clears the air path.
Computers turn electrical energy into useful work and heat. Cooling carries some of that heat away.
If temperatures become too high, hardware may reduce performance to protect itself.
A faster fan is not a magic upgrade. Clear airflow and a suitable workload help the whole system stay comfortable.

title: The Spare Copy
scenes: Pip carefully saves a story. Then the only drive breaks. Saving was helpful, but the story still disappears.
A backup is another copy that can help restore data after loss, damage, or a mistake.
A copy on the same failing device may disappear too. Separate locations reduce some shared risks.
Saving keeps your latest work. Backing up gives that work another chance when its first home fails.

title: The Falling Moon
scenes: Mochi asks why the Moon does not simply fall down to Earth. Pip draws a curved path.
Gravity pulls the Moon toward Earth, while its sideways motion keeps carrying it forward.
An orbit is continuous falling around another body, rather than falling straight onto its surface.
The Moon really is falling. Its path keeps missing the ground. Motion and gravity make the dance possible.

title: The Floating Lunch
scenes: Pip watches an astronaut's sandwich float. Has gravity vanished from the space station?
Gravity still acts strongly there. The station and everything inside it are falling around Earth together.
That shared free fall makes objects appear weightless relative to the station.
Floating does not mean gravity is absent. Sometimes everything around you is falling at the same time.

title: The Slow Sunbeam
scenes: Mochi waves at the Sun and expects an instant answer. Pip starts a very patient clock.
Light travels extremely fast, but the distance from the Sun to Earth is enormous.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us. The sunlight arriving now began its journey earlier.
Looking into space also means looking into the past. Even the nearest star sends us slightly old news.

title: The Moon's Wardrobe
scenes: Pip thinks the Moon changes shape every week. Mochi checks whether pieces are falling off.
The Sun always lights roughly half the Moon. From Earth, we see different portions of that lit half.
Those changing views create the familiar lunar phases. Earth's shadow is involved in lunar eclipses, not ordinary phases.
The Moon keeps its shape. Our viewing angle changes the bright shape we see in the sky.

title: The Tail That Pushed
scenes: Mochi's rocket cannot push against empty space. Pip wonders whether it needs a wall behind it.
A rocket throws exhaust backward. The exhaust pushes the rocket forward in response.
This exchange of momentum works in a vacuum. The rocket carries the material it needs to throw away.
A rocket does not need air to push against. Sending mass one way can send the rocket the other way.

title: The Blue Planet's Blanket
scenes: Pip builds a tiny planet with no atmosphere. The robot soon notices a very different world.
Earth's atmosphere contains gases that absorb and emit infrared radiation, helping warm the surface.
This natural greenhouse effect matters for life. Increasing greenhouse gases changes the planet's energy balance.
A blanket is only an analogy. The real story is about energy moving in and out of Earth's system.

title: The Star's Kitchen
scenes: Mochi thinks stars burn wooden fuel. Pip looks for a forest inside the Sun and finds none.
The Sun's energy mainly comes from nuclear fusion in its core, where hydrogen becomes helium.
A small amount of mass becomes energy. That energy eventually escapes into space as radiation.
A star is not a giant campfire. Its power comes from changes inside atomic nuclei, under extraordinary conditions.

title: The Planet Without a Floor
scenes: Pip packs hiking boots for Jupiter. Mochi asks exactly where the robot plans to stand.
Jupiter is a giant planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with deeper layers under enormous pressure.
It has no solid surface like Earth's ground. Its visible clouds are only the outer part.
A planet does not have to be rocky. Before packing your boots, ask what kind of world you are visiting.

title: The Quiet Explosion
scenes: Mochi watches a space film and hears a huge explosion. Pip carries a microphone into a vacuum.
Sound needs matter to carry its vibrations. In a vacuum, ordinary sound cannot travel between separated objects.
Light can cross that empty space, so an observer could see an explosion without hearing it through the vacuum.
Space can be visually dramatic and acoustically silent. A soundtrack is not always a physics lesson.

title: The Shadow Appointment
scenes: Pip wants to schedule a solar eclipse every month. Mochi notices that most new moons miss the Sun.
The Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's path around the Sun, so the alignment usually misses.
A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun in the right alignment.
The ingredients meet often, but the geometry must be right. An eclipse is a very particular shadow appointment.

title: The Seed's Packed Lunch
scenes: Mochi plants a seed in darkness and wonders how its first shoot can grow before making leaves.
Many seeds contain stored food that supports early growth after germination begins.
Suitable moisture, temperature, and often oxygen matter. The exact conditions depend on the plant species.
A seed carries a starting supply, not an unlimited lunch. Once leaves develop, light becomes central to its future growth.

title: The Leaf's Sun Kitchen
scenes: Pip offers a plant a bowl of soil for lunch. Mochi points at its green leaves instead.
During photosynthesis, plants use light energy to help make sugars from carbon dioxide and water.
Soil can supply water and mineral nutrients, but most of a plant's carbon comes from carbon dioxide.
A leaf is a tiny solar kitchen. The ingredients arrive from both the air and the roots.

title: The Flower Delivery
scenes: Mochi sees a bee leaving one flower and landing on another. Pip thinks it is simply sightseeing.
As bees visit flowers, pollen can stick to their bodies and travel to another flower.
Moving suitable pollen helps many flowering plants reproduce. Different plants use different pollinators or other methods.
The bee seeks food, while the flower may gain a delivery service. Nature often links two different needs.

title: The Underground Straw
scenes: Pip waters a plant's leaves but forgets its dry soil. Mochi looks below the surface for the problem.
Roots absorb water and minerals. Water can then move through the plant's water-conducting tissues.
Evaporation from leaves helps pull water upward through a connected column, alongside other effects.
The visible leaves tell only part of the story. A healthy plant depends on what happens underground too.

title: The Forest Clean-up Crew
scenes: Mochi sees fallen leaves piling up and asks why forests are not buried under endless old plants.
Fungi, bacteria, and other decomposers break down dead material, releasing nutrients into the ecosystem.
Decomposition takes time and depends on conditions such as temperature and moisture.
The forest has no rubbish truck. Its clean-up crew turns yesterday's living things into resources for tomorrow.

title: The Beaver's New Neighbours
scenes: Pip notices a beaver building a dam. Soon the surrounding water and habitats begin to change.
Beaver dams can slow flowing water and create wetlands, affecting many other organisms.
These changes can benefit some species and cause problems in particular locations. Ecosystems contain real tradeoffs.
One animal's building project can reshape a landscape. A habitat is something living things help create, not just occupy.

title: The Camouflage Contest
scenes: Mochi hides a bright toy on a green leaf. Pip spots it instantly, but misses a leaf-shaped insect.
Camouflage can make an organism harder to detect against its surroundings.
Predators and prey both use different strategies. A colour that helps in one setting may stand out in another.
Blending in is a relationship with the background. The best hiding costume depends on where the game is played.

title: The Bat's Echo Map
scenes: Pip turns off the lights and loses the path. A little bat keeps flying around the obstacles.
Many bats emit calls and listen for returning echoes, using them to locate objects and prey.
The delay and other features of the echo provide information about the surroundings.
An echo can be more than a repeated sound. For an echolocating bat, it is part of a moving map.

title: The Water-Saving Cactus
scenes: Mochi gives a cactus enormous soft leaves. Pip predicts a difficult day in the hot desert.
Many cacti store water in fleshy stems and have spines instead of ordinary broad leaves.
Their surfaces and gas-exchange strategies help reduce water loss, although adaptations vary among species.
Desert plants are not simply waiting for rain. Their shapes reflect the challenge of keeping precious water.

title: The Web of Lunches
scenes: Pip removes one insect from a toy ecosystem. Mochi notices that several hungry neighbours lose a meal.
A food web describes feeding relationships among organisms. Many species connect to more than one food source.
Changes can spread through those connections, although the exact effects depend on the ecosystem.
Nature is more like a web than a single chain. Tugging one thread can move several others.

title: The Spoon's Warm Journey
scenes: Mochi leaves a metal spoon in hot soup. Later, the handle feels warm even above the soup.
Thermal energy moves through the spoon by conduction, from warmer regions toward cooler ones.
Different materials transfer thermal energy at different rates. Metal often conducts it much faster than wood.
The handle did not need to touch the soup. Energy travelled through the connected material to reach it.

title: The Invisible Push
scenes: Pip rubs a balloon on a jumper, then watches it attract tiny pieces of paper.
Rubbing can transfer electric charge between materials. Charged objects can exert forces on nearby matter.
The paper can be attracted even if its overall charge is neutral, because charges inside it can shift slightly.
An invisible electric interaction can move visible things. A tiny experiment reveals forces beyond what our eyes can see.

title: The Mirror's Reply
scenes: Mochi shines a torch at a mirror and tries to catch the reflected beam.
For a flat mirror, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, measured from the normal.
The normal is an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface, not a line along the mirror.
The mirror follows a simple rule. Draw the right reference line and the reflected path becomes easier to predict.

title: The Heavy Feather Puzzle
scenes: Pip drops a feather and a stone. The stone lands first, so Mochi blames gravity alone.
In air, drag affects how objects fall. A feather experiences strong resistance relative to its weight.
Without air resistance, objects dropped together at the same place fall with the same gravitational acceleration.
A falling race tests more than gravity when air joins in. Remove the extra player before judging the rule.

title: The Bending Straw
scenes: Mochi dips a straight straw into water. Suddenly it looks bent at the surface.
Light changes direction when crossing between materials at an angle, because its speed changes.
This refraction changes where underwater objects appear to be. The straw itself can remain perfectly straight.
Our eyes follow arriving light. When the light bends, the picture can fool us about the object's position.

title: The Magnet's Two Ends
scenes: Pip cuts a pretend magnet in half, hoping to collect a lonely north pole.
An ordinary bar magnet has north and south poles. Cutting it makes smaller magnets, each with both poles.
Opposite magnetic poles attract, and matching poles repel. The field continues around each new piece.
Breaking a magnet does not give you ordinary isolated poles. You have made two smaller partners in the same dance.

title: The Sound Wave Parade
scenes: Mochi hits a drum and imagines bits of air flying all the way across the room.
Sound is a travelling disturbance. Nearby particles vibrate and pass the disturbance to their neighbours.
The particles do not need to make the whole journey from the drum to the listener.
A crowd can pass a wave around a stadium while people stay near their seats. Sound travels by a similar relay.

title: The Lever's Bargain
scenes: Pip cannot lift a heavy box. Mochi brings a long bar and puts a pivot beneath it.
A lever can trade a larger movement over a longer distance for a greater force over a shorter distance.
The arrangement of the load, effort, and pivot determines the mechanical advantage.
The lever does not create free energy. It changes the terms of the job so a small worker can do it.

title: The Floating Clay Boat
scenes: Mochi drops a clay ball into water. It sinks. Pip reshapes the same clay into a wide boat.
Water exerts an upward buoyant force related to the weight of displaced water.
The boat shape can displace more water before filling or sinking. Average density and shape both matter.
Floating is not decided by the material's name alone. The space an object occupies changes the water it pushes aside.

title: The Braking Skateboard
scenes: Pip rolls along a smooth path, then hits a rough patch and slows down.
Friction opposes relative sliding or the tendency to slide between contacting surfaces.
It can turn organised motion into thermal energy. It also helps shoes grip and brakes stop wheels.
Friction is not simply an enemy of motion. The same interaction that slows a skateboard helps its rider stand safely.

title: The Cloud's Suitcase
scenes: Mochi sees water vanish from a puddle and thinks the Sun has destroyed it.
Liquid water can evaporate into water vapour, an invisible gas in the air.
When moist air cools enough, water can condense into tiny droplets or ice crystals that form clouds.
The water changes form and location. The sky is part of a continuing journey, not a place where water disappears.

title: The Cold Glass Mystery
scenes: Pip fills a glass with icy water. Soon drops appear outside, although the glass has no leak.
Water vapour in the surrounding air can condense on the cold surface.
The droplets outside usually come from the air, not through the glass from the drink.
A cold surface can reveal invisible moisture. Sometimes the answer to a wet mystery is floating all around you.

title: The Ice Boat
scenes: Mochi watches ice float and asks why frozen water does not simply sink to the bottom.
Ordinary ice is less dense than liquid water because its molecular structure holds molecules farther apart.
That lower density lets ice float in liquid water under familiar conditions.
Freezing changes more than temperature. The arrangement of molecules helps explain a winter pond's floating roof.

title: The Raindrop Race
scenes: Pip draws raindrops as tiny pointed teardrops. Mochi checks what falling drops really look like.
Small raindrops are nearly spherical. Larger falling drops can flatten because of the air flowing around them.
Very large drops may break apart rather than keep growing into giant falling teardrops.
A familiar symbol is not always a realistic shape. Air and surface tension sculpt the drops on their way down.

title: The Salt That Stayed
scenes: Mochi warms salty water and catches the vapour on a cool lid. Where did the salt go?
During ordinary evaporation, water leaves as vapour while dissolved salts mostly remain behind.
Condensing that vapour can produce water with much less salt, the basic idea behind distillation.
Separation is possible because substances behave differently. But making drinkable water still requires suitable equipment and careful handling.

title: The River's Curved Road
scenes: Pip tries to make a river follow a perfectly straight line. The flowing water keeps shaping bends.
Moving water can erode material from some places and deposit it elsewhere.
In many bends, stronger erosion occurs along the outer bank while sediment builds toward the inner bank.
A river is both traveller and sculptor. Its path and the landscape keep changing each other over time.

title: The Hidden Water Table
scenes: Mochi imagines all groundwater inside one enormous underground lake. Pip looks at a sponge instead.
Much groundwater occupies pores and cracks in soil and rock, rather than a vast open cave.
The water table marks the upper surface of a saturated zone in the ground.
There can be water where you see only stone. Tiny connected spaces can store and carry a remarkable amount.

title: The Snowflake Workshop
scenes: Pip wants every snowflake to have the same shape. Mochi changes the temperature and humidity.
Ice crystals grow as water vapour joins their structure. Growth conditions influence their detailed shapes.
The crystal structure favours sixfold symmetry, while changing conditions create many variations.
A snowflake records part of its journey through a cloud. Similar building rules can create wonderfully different results.

title: The Ocean's Moving Belt
scenes: Mochi pours warm and cold water into a model ocean. Pip notices that density can change the motion.
Temperature and salinity affect seawater density. Density differences help drive parts of ocean circulation.
Winds also drive major surface currents. Real ocean movement involves several connected processes.
The ocean is not a still bowl. Heat, salt, wind, and Earth's rotation help keep its enormous waters moving.

title: The Rising Tide Clock
scenes: Pip thinks the ocean breathes in and out every day. Mochi invites the Moon into the explanation.
Differences in the Moon's gravitational pull across Earth help produce tides. The Sun contributes too.
Coastlines, ocean basins, and local conditions change the timing and height of the tides people see.
The tide is a local response to a planet-wide interaction. The same sky can produce different shorelines' schedules.

title: The Two Ice-Cream Clues
scenes: Mochi notices more ice-cream sales and more swimmers on hot days. Did ice cream push everyone into the sea?
Two quantities can rise together because a third factor influences both. Here, hot weather is a possible common cause.
A correlation can suggest a question, but it does not establish that one thing causes the other.
Before drawing an arrow between two events, look for another explanation that could connect them both.

title: The Lucky Coin
scenes: Pip flips five heads in a row. Mochi declares that the next flip must finally be tails.
For independent fair coin flips, earlier results do not change the probability of the next result.
The next flip still has equal chances of heads and tails, despite a surprising-looking streak.
Randomness does not keep a short-term balancing notebook. A streak can be unusual without making the next flip owe us anything.

title: The Cropped Photograph
scenes: Mochi sees one corner of a photo and thinks a robot stole the whole cake.
Pip widens the image. The robot was carrying the cake to the birthday table.
A claim can change when missing context appears. A true fragment may still support a misleading impression.
Before judging a clip or screenshot, ask what happened before, what happened after, and what the frame leaves out.

title: The Test With Two Changes
scenes: Pip gives one plant more light and more water. It grows taller, so Mochi declares that light caused everything.
When several conditions change together, it is harder to identify which change explains the result.
A controlled comparison tries to keep other relevant conditions similar while testing a particular difference.
A good experiment is a carefully asked question. Change fewer things at once so the answer becomes easier to interpret.

title: The Tiny Opinion Poll
scenes: Mochi asks three friends whether everyone loves robot music. All three agree. Is the whole city convinced?
A sample can be too small or unrepresentative to support a broad conclusion.
Who was asked, how they were chosen, and how the question was worded all matter.
More answers can help, but selection matters too. Asking only your bandmates may still give a distorted picture.

title: The Average Monster
scenes: Pip shares a room with one extremely wealthy robot. The average wealth suddenly looks enormous.
The mean adds values and divides by their count. Extreme values can move it strongly.
The median is the middle value after sorting. It can tell a different story about a typical member.
An average is a tool, not the whole picture. Ask which average is being used and what the distribution looks like.

title: The Survivor's Workshop
scenes: Mochi studies only successful inventors and copies their strange hats. Pip looks for the inventors who failed.
If we examine only survivors or winners, we can miss information about those that did not make it.
A habit shared by winners may also be common among failures, so it may explain little.
Success stories can inspire a question. A fair investigation also asks which missing cases would change the answer.

title: The Broken Chart Ladder
scenes: Pip draws two bars with slightly different values. Mochi cuts off the bottom and makes the gap look enormous.
A chart's axis range can change the visual impression of a difference.
Labels, units, scale, and missing data help determine what a chart actually supports.
Read the ladder before comparing the heights. A dramatic picture can show a real but much smaller change.

title: The Opposite Test
scenes: Mochi invents a rule that every shiny rock is metal. Pip brings a shiny piece of glass.
One clear counterexample can disprove a universal claim, even if many earlier examples seemed to fit.
That does not make every weaker or related claim false. The exact wording matters.
Good reasoning tests a rule where it might fail. Looking only for friendly examples makes an idea harder to check.

title: The Confidence Dial
scenes: Pip hears a robot speak very confidently and assumes every answer must be correct.
Confidence and accuracy are different things. A fluent explanation can still contain errors or unsupported claims.
Checking evidence, sources, and reasoning matters more than how certain the speaker sounds.
Turn your trust dial with evidence. A careful answer that admits uncertainty can be more useful than a bold guess.

title: The Halfway Library
scenes: Mochi searches a sorted shelf one book at a time. Pip opens the book in the middle instead.
If the target comes earlier, the search keeps the earlier half. Otherwise, it keeps the later half.
Repeating this halving process is binary search. It requires an ordered collection and suitable access to its middle.
A smart question can remove many possibilities at once. Organisation turns a long hunt into a few decisions.

title: The Double Rice Puzzle
scenes: Pip puts one grain on a square, then doubles the amount on each new square.
Doubling creates exponential growth. The increase becomes larger as the starting quantity grows.
It can look slow at first and then become enormous. The growth rule matters more than the first impression.
Before trusting your intuition, count a few more steps. Repeated multiplication can outrun an ordinary straight-line guess.

title: The Missing Unit
scenes: Mochi reports that a robot travelled at sixty. Pip cannot tell whether that means fast walking or a rocket.
A number needs units and context to describe a physical quantity. Metres per second differs from kilometres per hour.
Conversions preserve the underlying quantity while changing the numerical representation.
A bare number can hide a big misunderstanding. Carry the unit with the answer, just as a parcel needs its address.

title: The Area Rug
scenes: Pip doubles the width and length of a square rug. Mochi orders only twice as much material.
Area depends on two dimensions. Doubling both length and width makes the area four times as large.
Changing a linear size does not change every related quantity by the same factor.
Draw the new squares before buying the fabric. A small scaling rule can have a surprisingly large consequence.

title: The Percentage Trap
scenes: Mochi raises a price by fifty percent, then cuts the new price by fifty percent.
The second percentage uses a different starting amount. For example, one hundred becomes one hundred fifty, then seventy-five.
Equal-looking percentage changes do not necessarily cancel when their bases differ.
Always ask: a percentage of what? The hidden starting value is part of the calculation, not an optional detail.

title: The Weighted Backpack
scenes: Pip averages two class scores equally, even though one class has ten students and the other has thirty.
To find the overall student average, class averages must be weighted by the number of students they represent.
A small group and a large group should not automatically contribute the same amount.
An average of averages can mislead. Check whether every value stands for the same number of underlying observations.

title: The Map's Tiny World
scenes: Mochi follows a map and expects one centimetre on paper to mean one centimetre on the road.
A map scale relates distances in the representation to distances in the real world.
For a simple scale drawing, multiplying by the scale factor converts a map length into its corresponding real distance.
A map is useful because it changes size consistently. Read the scale before planning how far your feet must travel.

title: The Pattern Guess
scenes: Pip sees two, four, six, and predicts eight. Mochi asks whether any other rule could fit.
A short list can be explained by many different rules. A plausible continuation is not automatically the only possible one.
Extra context or a stated rule makes the problem more specific.
Patterns are invitations to make hypotheses. To know which hypothesis was intended, we sometimes need more than a few examples.

title: The Probability Garden
scenes: Mochi calls a chance of one in ten impossible. Pip plants ten pretend seeds and watches the surprises.
A low probability means an event is less likely, not forbidden. Repeated opportunities can make rare events worth considering.
It also does not guarantee one success in every ten tries. Chance is not a fixed schedule.
Treat probability as a measure of uncertainty. It helps expectations, but it does not write each individual outcome in advance.

title: The Rounding Relay
scenes: Pip rounds every little measurement early. By the end, Mochi's carefully planned shelf no longer fits.
Rounding changes values slightly. Repeating calculations with rounded intermediate values can accumulate error.
Keeping enough precision until the final result often reduces avoidable differences.
A tidy number is not always the best working number. Keep useful detail during the journey and round thoughtfully at the end.

title: The Robot's Guessing Game
scenes: Mochi asks an AI for a story. Pip imagines a tiny librarian choosing a perfect finished answer.
A language model generates text by using learned patterns to predict possible next tokens in context.
A token can be a word, part of a word, or another text fragment. Generation continues step by step.
Fluent text can emerge from this process, but fluency alone does not prove that the answer is true.

title: The Confident Wrong Door
scenes: Pip asks an AI for a fact it does not know. The answer sounds polished, but points to the wrong door.
AI systems can produce incorrect or invented details, sometimes called hallucinations.
Providing relevant sources and checking important claims can reduce mistakes, but no method guarantees every answer.
Use AI as a helpful participant in the investigation. For important facts, follow the evidence beyond the smooth sentence.

title: The Example Teacher
scenes: Mochi teaches a robot to recognise fruit using only pictures of red apples.
A model learns patterns from training examples. Narrow or unrepresentative examples can lead to poor performance elsewhere.
A green apple or an unfamiliar background may expose what the model actually learned.
Better examples cover the situations the system will face. Teaching is not just collecting more of the same picture.

title: The Homework Mirror
scenes: Pip trains a model on the practice questions, then celebrates perfect scores on those same questions.
Performance on familiar training data does not reliably show how well a model will handle new cases.
Separate evaluation data helps test generalisation. Careful evaluation also checks that training information has not leaked into the test.
A useful test asks something the learner has not already memorised. Otherwise, the score may mostly measure the mirror.

title: The Prompt With a Map
scenes: Mochi asks for something interesting and gets a vague answer. Pip adds a clear goal and useful background.
A prompt can specify the task, audience, relevant context, and desired format.
Examples or constraints can help, but instructions do not give a model knowledge or capabilities it does not have.
A clear question is a map for the answer. After improving the map, still check where the answer actually goes.

title: The Search Backpack
scenes: Pip gives an AI a backpack of relevant documents before asking it to explain a topic.
Retrieval-augmented generation brings selected external information into the model's context for a response.
Retrieval can help ground an answer, but the documents may be outdated, irrelevant, or misunderstood.
A source in the backpack is not a guarantee. Check whether the answer's claims really match what the source says.

title: The Biased Sorting Hat
scenes: Mochi builds a sorting robot using examples from only one corner of town.
Data, labels, design choices, and deployment conditions can all contribute to unfair or uneven results.
Measuring performance across relevant groups can reveal problems hidden by a single overall score.
A fairer system needs careful questions and ongoing checks. One impressive average cannot describe everyone's experience.

title: The Picture in Pieces
scenes: Pip zooms into a digital picture and discovers a grid of coloured squares.
A raster image represents visual information as pixels. Each pixel stores colour information according to an encoding.
Models can learn relationships between visual patterns and descriptions, but recognition can fail in unfamiliar conditions.
Seeing a pattern is not the same as understanding everything in a scene. Look closely at what the system actually identified.

title: The Context Suitcase
scenes: Mochi tells a robot a very long story, then wonders why an early detail is missing from the reply.
A model's context window limits how much input and output it can consider in a single interaction.
Applications choose what information to include. A long conversation does not necessarily mean every detail is always available.
Keep essential instructions and facts visible in the current task. Even a large suitcase has a limited capacity.

title: The Human Checkpoint
scenes: Pip lets an AI draft a bridge explanation. Mochi asks who will check the important engineering claims.
AI can help brainstorm, summarise, and draft. Responsibility for important decisions still needs appropriate human review.
The right checks depend on the consequences of an error and the expertise the task requires.
A useful assistant can speed up work. A sensible checkpoint helps make sure that faster work is also reliable.

title: The Battery Backpack
scenes: Mochi calls a battery a box of electricity. Pip looks for the process that makes current possible.
A battery stores energy chemically. Chemical reactions can drive electric charge through a connected circuit.
Charging a rechargeable battery uses outside energy to reverse some of those chemical changes.
A battery is a portable energy system. It cannot supply unlimited energy just because its wires form a loop.

title: The Open Circuit
scenes: Pip builds a lamp circuit but leaves a gap. Mochi shakes the battery, and the lamp stays dark.
For a simple steady current, charge needs a complete conducting path through the circuit.
Closing the switch completes that path. Opening it interrupts the circuit and stops the lamp's ordinary operation.
The switch does not create energy. It controls whether the circuit offers a connected route for charge to flow.

title: The Solar Lunch
scenes: Mochi points a solar panel at the sky and waits for it to collect heat like a soup pot.
Photovoltaic cells convert some incoming light energy into electrical energy.
Their output depends on factors including light levels, panel orientation, and temperature. They do not work equally well in every condition.
A solar panel's job is conversion, not creating energy from nothing. Sunshine provides the incoming energy for the system.

title: The Windmill's Trade
scenes: Pip builds a wind turbine and wonders whether making it spin faster can create endless power.
A turbine extracts some energy from moving air. Its blades and generator convert part of that energy into electricity.
Wind conditions, turbine design, and operating limits affect the output.
The wind supplies the energy. Clever engineering helps capture some of it while keeping the machine within safe limits.

title: The LED's Bright Bargain
scenes: Mochi compares two lamps that give similar useful light. One uses much less electrical power.
Efficiency compares useful output with input. LEDs can produce useful light with less energy than older incandescent lamps.
Some energy still becomes heat, and real efficiency depends on the device and conditions.
Doing the same useful job with less input is an efficiency gain. Brightness and power are related, but they are not identical.

title: The Insulated House
scenes: Pip heats a tiny house, but warmth keeps escaping. Mochi adds insulation around its walls.
Insulation reduces the rate of heat transfer. It can help a building stay warm or cool with less energy.
It does not generate heat or stop every possible loss. Air leaks and windows can matter too.
The best heater is only part of the story. Keeping useful energy where it is needed can change the whole job.

title: The Regenerating Ride
scenes: Mochi watches an electric vehicle slow down. Pip notices that some energy can return to the battery.
Regenerative braking uses the motor as a generator, converting some motion energy into electrical energy.
It cannot recover everything, and ordinary braking may still be needed depending on conditions.
Slowing down usually spends motion. A regenerative system can save part of that energy for a later journey.

title: The Transformer's Neighbours
scenes: Pip wants to move electrical power a long distance. Mochi worries about energy lost as heat in wires.
For the same transmitted power, higher voltage allows lower current, which can reduce resistive losses.
Transformers help change alternating-current voltage levels so electricity can be transmitted and then used appropriately.
The journey and the destination need different conditions. Power networks change voltage along the way to make both possible.

title: The Power-Time Mix-up
scenes: Mochi reads a device's watt label and thinks it tells the total energy used all day.
Power is the rate of energy transfer. Energy use also depends on how long the device operates.
A low-power device running for many hours can use more energy than a higher-power device running briefly.
To estimate the energy bill, bring a clock as well as a power label. Rate and total answer different questions.

title: The Energy Relay
scenes: Pip follows energy from sunlight to a plant, then to food, and finally to a moving robot demonstration.
Energy can be transferred and transformed between different forms. It is conserved in a closed system.
In real processes, energy often becomes more spread out, making some of it less useful for the intended job.
Energy does not disappear when the useful motion stops. Ask where it went and how available it is now.
